content.body: Have you ever played a word game where you change one letter at a time to transform one word into another? That's called a Word Ladder! Today we'll learn how to find the shortest transformation path between words using a clever approach. You'll discover how to track what you've already seen to avoid unnecessary work.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why tracking visited words is essential for finding shortest paths
2. Implement a breadth-first search approach using a queue
3. Use a Set data structure to remember words you've already processed
4. Generate valid neighbor words by changing one letter at a time
5. Return the shortest transformation sequence between two words
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. We want to transform 'hit' into 'cog' using only valid English words, changing one letter at a time. Which word would you try first after 'hit'?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: What's a valid English word that differs from 'hit' by just one letter?
content.successMessage: Great! 'hot' is a valid next step since it changes 'i' to 'o'.

content.title: Try a longer chain
content.prompt: From 'hot', what word gets us closer to 'cog'?
content.successMessage: Nice! 'dot' changes 'h' to 'd' and gets us closer to 'cog'.

content.title: One more step
content.prompt: From 'dot', what word gets us to 'cog'?
content.successMessage: Perfect! 'dog' changes 't' to 'g'. Then 'cog' changes 'd' to 'c' to complete the ladder: hit → hot → dot → dog → cog.

content.body: What you just did was explore possibilities step by step, trying different one-letter changes. You intuitively avoided repeating words you'd already seen (like not going back to 'hit' once you had 'hot'). This manual checking works for short ladders, but gets complex quickly.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When words are longer or the dictionary is large, manually tracking which words you've tried becomes overwhelming. You might revisit the same word multiple times or miss shorter paths. We need a systematic way to explore possibilities while remembering what we've already seen. Can't figure out how? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to use a lookup structure to remember seen values and avoid re-scanning. For Word Ladder, we'll use a Set to track words we've already visited. This acts like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. We store words as keys (values aren't needed for simple existence checks). We check the structure before adding new words to explore, and add to it immediately after processing a word.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use breadth-first search (BFS) with a queue to explore words level by level, ensuring we find the shortest path. The Set will prevent cycles and redundant work.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Create a queue starting with the beginWord
2. Create a Set to track visited words
3. While queue has items:
   a. Take the current transformation sequence
   b. Get the last word in the sequence
   c. Generate all valid one-letter changes
   d. For each valid neighbor not in visited:
      - If it's the endWord, return sequence + neighbor
      - Add to visited and enqueue new sequence
4. Return 0 if no path found
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the data structures
steps.instruction: Create the initial queue and visited Set. The queue should start with an array containing just the beginWord, since that's our starting transformation sequence.
steps.hint: Use an array for the queue, with the first element being an array containing beginWord. Create a new Set and add beginWord to it.
steps.expectedOutcome: Queue initialized with [[beginWord]], visited Set contains beginWord
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the foundation for our BFS approach.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember the queue should contain sequences, not just words.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a queue that starts with an array containing beginWord, and a Set to track visited words.

steps.title: Create the BFS loop
steps.instruction: Set up a while loop that continues as long as there are items in the queue. Inside, we'll process each transformation sequence.
steps.hint: Use while(queue.length > 0) to continue processing while there are sequences to explore.
steps.expectedOutcome: While loop that continues while queue has items
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The loop will process all possible transformation sequences.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your loop condition checks if the queue has any items.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a loop that runs while there are sequences to process in the queue.

steps.title: Process current sequence
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, get the current transformation sequence from the front of the queue, and get the last word in that sequence (the word we need to transform from).
steps.hint: Use shift() to get the first sequence from queue, then get the last element of that sequence.
steps.expectedOutcome: Current sequence and current word extracted
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we have the word we need to transform from.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Remember we need both the sequence and the last word in it.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to get the first sequence from the queue, then get the last word from that sequence.

steps.title: Generate neighbor words
steps.instruction: Create a helper section to generate all possible one-letter changes for the current word. For each position in the word, try every letter from 'a' to 'z'.
steps.hint: Use nested loops: one for each character position, and one for each possible letter replacement.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that generates all possible one-letter variations
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! This will generate all possible transformations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're getting there. Remember to try every letter at every position.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to generate new words by changing each character to every other letter.

steps.title: Check and process valid neighbors
steps.instruction: For each generated neighbor, check if it's in the wordList and not already visited. If it's the endWord, return the sequence length. Otherwise, add to visited and enqueue the new sequence.
steps.hint: Convert wordList to a Set for O(1) lookup. Check if neighbor exists and isn't visited before processing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're handling the core logic of checking and tracking visited words.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Remember to check both wordSet and visited, and handle the endWord case.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check if the neighbor is valid, not visited, and handle when we find the endWord.

steps.title: Handle no solution case
steps.instruction: After the BFS loop completes without finding the endWord, return 0 to indicate no transformation sequence exists.
steps.hint: Add a return 0 statement after the while loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: Return 0 when no path is found
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've completed the Word Ladder solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. We need to return something when no path exists.
steps.feedbackWrong: If we exit the loop without finding endWord, we should return 0.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented a Word Ladder solver using BFS with a visited Set. Remember: the key insight was using a lookup structure (Set) to remember seen words and avoid re-processing. This 'notebook' approach lets us check in one step whether we've already explored a word. The BFS ensures we find the shortest path, while the Set prevents cycles. What to remember: always check your lookup structure before adding new items, and add to it immediately after processing to maintain correctness.
